A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NFH-SEM work, and their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. However, v1 references separate Supplementary Information that is absent from its PDF, limiting exact comparison of its real-data ablations and 3Q-BSE experiments with v2's included appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original SEM reconstructions of TPL microstructures, peach pollen, and silicon carbide, together with simulation results and quantitative ablations in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 retains original real-data and simulation results and reports additional learning-based comparisons and initialization-robustness experiments in Figures 5, G3, and G4.

M1.justification: The hash-encoded SDF network, fourth-order BSE forward model, quadrant-specific parameters, loss terms, iterative shadow masking, and three-stage optimization are retained. Alternative geometric initializers are evaluated using the existing pipeline; no new proposed algorithm component is established.

E1.justification: The real Wukong, Lucy, Lion, peach-pollen, and SiC coverage and CAD-based 4Q-BSE simulations remain the same. v1 already references 3Q-BSE experiments, but their missing supplementary material prevents verification of whether the precise simulated coverage in v2 Appendix G.4 is unchanged. Added initialization algorithms alone do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The conventional SfM/Metashape and PS comparisons are retained under revised labels. v2 additionally evaluates NeuS, 2DGS, PGSR, DN-Splatter, VGGT, and MapAnything in Section 4.2 and Figures 5/G4, plus GeoMVSNet and MVSFormer++ in Appendix G.1/Figure G3. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator families.

E3.justification: The principal simulated geometry metric changes from depth MAE in micrometers to Chamfer distance in nanometers. v2 also introduces evaluations using DTU-pretrained MVS models and a robustness protocol that substitutes their reconstructions for the usual initialization. The retained NFH-SEM acquisition and training settings, including 37 viewpoints and 3,000 iterations, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G.2/Figure G3 adds a distinct initialization-robustness analysis using noisy, incomplete GeoMVSNet and MVSFormer++ reconstructions across the real specimens. The four original component ablations remain. Real-TPL ablations and 3Q-BSE tests were already referenced in v1, so their inclusion in v2 is not sufficient evidence that those analyses are new.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across training runs. Reconstruction confidence weights and simulated image-noise specifications are not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 replaces depth-MAE results, including the 0.58 micrometer NFH-SEM average, with Chamfer results averaging 17.48 nm; these are different metrics, not a performance gain. It adds learned-baseline and alternative-initialization reconstructions and reports 782 nm pollen features and 1.559 micrometer SiC steps. Shared normal-error and BSE-model-error values remain unchanged; 81.71% versus 81.7% shadow accuracy is equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: The BSE emission derivation, polynomial model, SDF constraints, optimization equations, and custom BSE/shadow metrics remain mathematically equivalent. The PS gradient equation is algebraically rearranged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive formal assumption is introduced; the standard geometry-metric substitution belongs to E3.

C1.justification: The central claims of continuous hybrid reconstruction, detector self-calibration, and shadow separation remain. v2 adds an explicit claim to the first multi-view, multi-detector SEM dataset and extends claimed superiority to learning-based reconstruction methods, without redefining the underlying methodological contribution.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's edge-effect, charging, and Lambertian-model limitations, v2 discusses material-dependent emission and geometry shadowed across every quadrant. Appendix D explains limitations of reference metrology and why fabrication CAD is unsuitable as real-sample ground truth. Section 4.3 explicitly restricts the simulation's applicability to hybrid-stage ablations, and new comparisons receive domain-gap and imaging-physics interpretations.

D1.justification: Most acquisition, architecture, hardware, and hyperparameter details are retained or relocated. v2 adds an explicit code/real-dataset availability statement and repository link, and clarifies normalized view-count confidence weights. Conversely, v1's Metashape and grad2Surf version numbers and fixed 0.2 simulation confidence are omitted; this does not establish changed implementations.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially expands positioning around learned SfM/MVS, feed-forward reconstruction, and Gaussian splatting, including VGGT, MapAnything, and 2DGS. v2 emphasizes SEM domain shift and physics-specific modeling, and adds metrology references supporting the ground-truth discussion. These exceed citation renumbering or publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The Results–Discussion–Methods organization becomes numbered Related Work, Method, Experiments, and Conclusion sections, with substantial technical material moved into appendices. Sample-specific narratives are consolidated and terminology is revised throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adds an opening application figure and learning-based comparison displays, combines v1 Figures 2–4 into a compact comparison matrix, and merges three quantitative tables into one. Workflow and simulation figures are reformatted, and appendix figures present additional comparisons. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: The learned-method comparisons and initialization tests strengthen validation beyond v1's conventional baselines, while the expanded limitations and ground-truth discussion improve transparency. The gain is limited: real-data comparisons remain qualitative and use different input information, Chamfer results do not establish improved reconstruction performance, and some reproducibility details are omitted. The core method and shared quantitative findings remain unchanged.
